stories.title: When a Rail Park Can Serve a Community, Not Displace It
stories.summary: Cities are turning abandoned rail lines into parks — and this time, organizers are building in protections so longtime residents aren't priced out. From Philadelphia to Chicago to DC, community land trusts and neighborhood plans are putting locals first.
stories.extended_summary: Philadelphia's Rail Park raised nearby property values after just its first quarter mile — so organizers wrote a Community First Plan to drive what comes next. In Chicago's South Side, the AgroEco District aims to protect Black homeowners and keep construction jobs in the neighborhood, which leader Anton Seals Jr. calls reparative justice. And DC's 11th Street Bridge Park led to a community land trust now holding 262 housing units. The shared stance: not against development, but against development that displaces the people who already live there.

stories.title: “Bin It to Win It”: Dalton launches neighborhood recycling showdown
stories.summary: Dalton, Georgia turned recycling into a neighborhood showdown called 'Bin It to Win It.' North Oaks beat North Summit with over 60% household participation — taking home custom dishcloths and bragging-rights yard signs.
stories.extended_summary: Two Dalton, Georgia neighborhoods went head-to-head to see who could recycle more — and North Oaks took the crown with over 60 percent of households setting out their bins. 'Bin It to Win It,' organized by Keep Dalton-Whitfield Beautiful, tracked participation street by street, with city drivers logging who rolled out at least one recycling bin. The prize: a custom Swedish dishcloth for every household, victory yard signs at the neighborhood entrance, and local media glory. 'We wanted to take something routine and make it fun,' said coordinator Amy Hartline — and it worked.

stories.title: A Different World
stories.summary: The Pocahontas Reframed Film Festival turns 10 this year — now the largest Native American film festival on the East Coast. What started with 13 films has grown to 52 across five days, with Indigenous filmmakers from the U.S., Brazil, and Australia. Founder Bradby Brown built it by first meeting with all 11 state-recognized Virginia tribes. 'We're telling the true story of our history.'
stories.extended_summary: Before launching the Pocahontas Reframed Film Festival, director Bradby Brown sat down with the chiefs of all 11 state-recognized tribes in Virginia to make sure they were on board. A decade later, it's the largest Native American film festival on the East Coast — grown from 13 films to 52 across five days, with Indigenous filmmakers from the U.S., Brazil, and Australia. The festival takes its name from the most recognized Native American woman in the country, and its mission is to reframe the story most people learned from a Disney movie. 'We're telling the true story of our history, and basically the effects of colonization on Indigenous people,' Brown says.

stories.title: A Little Swap Became a Big Idea: Creative Reuse Montana Is Ready for Its Next Chapter
stories.summary: Creative Reuse Montana started as a craft supply swap two years ago. Now it's a secondhand arts shop, a workshop space, and a community hub — and it's diverted more than 18,556 pounds of supplies from the waste stream, powered by 1,459 volunteer hours. Teachers, schools, and memory care centers all benefit. Creativity, made accessible.
stories.extended_summary: What began as a small craft supply swap two years ago has become a secondhand arts and crafts shop, a workshop space, and a gathering place in Montana. Since October 2025, Creative Reuse Montana has diverted more than 18,556 pounds of creative supplies from the waste stream and put them back into the hands of teachers, schools, memory care centers, and local businesses. Volunteers have logged 1,459 hours sorting, organizing, and welcoming people through the door. People have found affordable materials for school projects, supplies for small businesses, and handmade gift inspiration — plus something just as valuable: connection. It's a community institution in the making.

stories.title: AMEN builds Great Lakes team to expand free dental care
stories.summary: AMEN is building a dedicated Michigan team so free dental clinics can reach more Great Lakes residents who've gone years without care. A Delta Dental Foundation grant means local volunteers and equipment stay in the region instead of waiting on one traveling crew.
stories.extended_summary: People were lining up at 5 a.m. — hours before the doors opened — just to get a tooth pulled. Janelle Randall of AMEN remembers every chair filled all day with extractions and fillings, patients of all ages who'd gone years without dental care. Now a Delta Dental Foundation grant is letting the nonprofit build a permanent Michigan team with equipment kept right in the Great Lakes region, so clinics can happen more often without depending on a single crew crisscrossing the country.

stories.title: Aging Sisters of St. Agnes turn to Bernardine Franciscans to preserve Catholic university's mission
stories.summary: With a median age of 82 and only 111 sisters left, the Sisters of St. Agnes turned to another order to keep their beloved Marian University alive. The Bernardine Franciscans stepped in to help preserve the Catholic school's mission for the next generation.
stories.extended_summary: The Sisters of St. Agnes have 111 members and a median age of 82 — and a university they founded in 1936 that they can't carry alone forever. So they reached out to the Bernardine Franciscan Sisters, who'd been watching Catholic colleges close across the country and wanted to help one survive. The partnership is a quiet act of faith: one aging congregation entrusting its life's work to another, determined that Marian University's mission outlast them both.

stories.title: Area colleges expand services for veterans
stories.summary: Grossmont and Cuyamaca colleges served over 1,500 veterans and military-affiliated students this year, with visits up 25% and counseling up 16%. Cuyamaca is also about to become the first community college in the country to partner with Service2Schools.
stories.extended_summary: Since Marine Corps veteran Gregory Pace took over Grossmont's Veterans Resource Center last fall, visits jumped 25% and counseling sessions rose 16% — proof that when you actually promote the help, people show up. Across the district, the two colleges have served more than 1,500 veterans and military-affiliated students this year. And Cuyamaca is on the verge of becoming the first community college in the nation to formally partner with Service2Schools, opening a real pathway for student veterans to transfer to top universities.

stories.title: As the Muslim population grows swiftly in the US, a Berwyn mosque is flourishing
stories.summary: After 26 years of searching for a space that felt like both Islam and home, Raul Gonzalez and Imam Christopher Pavlicek opened Ojala Islamic Center in Berwyn — the Midwest's first Latino-led mosque, founded on the first day of Ramadan.
stories.extended_summary: For 26 years, Raul Gonzalez looked for a place where he could be fully Latino and fully Muslim at once — and never found it. So he and Christopher Pavlicek, who felt the same ache, found a shuttered church in Berwyn and opened Ojala Islamic Center on the first day of Ramadan: the Midwest's first Latino-led mosque. 'Nobody's doing it,' Pavlicek says. 'I have to do it myself.' It arrives as the U.S. Muslim population grows swiftly — and as Latino converts finally get a home that honors both halves of who they are.

stories.title: Aspen Landscapers Let the Bots Do the Paperwork so the Crew Stays on the Lawn
stories.summary: Aspen landscaper Jeff Margulies deployed AI across a dozen parts of his business so his 60-to-70-person crew can stay on the lawn instead of buried in paperwork. Real-time job costing, progress photos, and automated scheduling have helped Good Earth grow sixfold.
stories.extended_summary: Jeff Margulies calls it "tickling the bots." The Aspen landscaper has wired Claude-based AI into roughly a dozen parts of Good Earth Landscaping—from field photos and clock-ins to real-time job costing checked against the budget on the spot. The goal isn't fewer workers; it's keeping his 60-to-70-person crew on the lawn instead of drowning in admin. Since he bought into the company in 2018, Good Earth has grown sixfold, and the paperwork now mostly handles itself.

stories.title: Boys & Girls Clubs of Delaware connects youth learning, local farms and fresh food
stories.summary: At the Western Sussex Boys & Girls Club, a celery-and-electrolytes lesson turned into a footrace — part of a Farm to Kitchen initiative bringing Delaware-grown food and hands-on nutrition education to kids.
stories.extended_summary: A lesson about celery turned into a lesson about the human body at the Western Sussex Boys & Girls Club — and then into a race. Students assigned to run 'without electrolytes' had to shuffle while their classmates sprinted, and some of the fastest runners lost. It's one example of the Farm to Kitchen Feeding Initiative, which brings Delaware-grown food to kids across Kent and Sussex counties while teaching them how plants grow and how food fuels their bodies. Lessons run from kindergarten through high school, with pre-K next. 'Sitting some more is just not helpful,' said educator Alana Carver, who builds movement into every session.

stories.title: Castle Dale celebrates grand opening of new community-backed all-abilities park
stories.summary: Castle Dale just opened an all-abilities park with wheelchair ramps, sensory areas, and swings every kid can use. The wild part? A young cowboy raised over $6,000 for it by hosting goat-tying events in honor of his friend Ruger, who has Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
stories.extended_summary: A kid with a love of rodeo turned goat-tying into a fundraiser for his friend — and helped build a park where every child can play. When Axel Mead heard Castle Dale was planning an all-abilities park, he thought of his friend Ruger Henrie, who has Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Axel set a $500 goal, but his goat-tying jackpot events blew past it, and every champion gave their prize money back. In total he raised over $6,000. Nineteen months after the idea was sketched on a napkin, the park opened with wheelchair-accessible ramps, sensory areas, and swings for all.
